On the last day of the municipal sound archive, a woman came in asking for the noise a particular swimming pool made at four in the afternoon.

“Underwater or above?” I asked.

She set her bag on the counter. “You have both?”

“We have underwater at four-oh-six. Above, there’s a gap between three-fifty and four-twenty. The lifeguard taped over it with his band.”

“They any good?”

“They get better.”

She thought about this. “Underwater, then.”

I brought out the headphones with the intact foam and found the file. The pool had closed twenty-three years earlier. I knew the recording well enough to identify the slap of the vacuum hose against the ladder and the little descending roar of someone doing a cannonball. At the end, the man holding the microphone came up for air and said, very distinctly, “Cold where the sun isn’t.”

The woman listened twice.

“Can I take it home?”

I glanced at the notice taped to the counter. We’d been told not to distribute material while the council decided what to do with the collection. The council had given itself six months to decide and us until five o’clock to leave the building.

“Have you got your phone?” I asked.

She took a blue flash drive from her bag instead. It was attached to an enormous brass key.

“Swimming pool key,” she said when she saw me looking. “They never asked for it back.”

“You worked there?”

“I lived there. My dad was the caretaker. There was a flat behind the changing rooms.” She put a finger on the key, still plugged into my computer. “Does the person holding the microphone say anything else?”

I played her the beginning, where the man cleared his throat. Then I found the above-water recording from three-forty, in which he asked somebody named Gary whether the lead would reach.

“Dad,” she said, fondly and with some exasperation, as if he’d just come in wearing shoes she’d asked him to throw away.

I made her a folder. While the files copied, she told me the flat had no windows on the pool side, for privacy, but if you sat on the kitchen counter with your feet in the sink you could look through a vent and see a little square of water. She’d done her homework there in summer until her father caught her and made her scrub the heel marks off the draining board.

“I thought we were poor,” she said. “Well, we were. But imagine getting home from school and having a pool.”

I asked if she wanted the lifeguard’s band too.

“Absolutely not,” she said. “That was Gary.”

After she left, I ate my lunch on a packing crate. Downstairs, someone dragged a desk across the tile in short, furious installments. There was still half a roll of red stickers on my desk, which we were supposed to put on things that belonged to the council. I stuck one to my apple.

At three, my brother called. He wanted to know if I’d changed my mind about the piano.

Our mother had been dead for nine weeks. In that time we’d found homes for seven dining chairs, an exercise bicycle, and a freezer full of plums. The piano was the only thing we both wanted and neither could take.

“The school can collect it Tuesday,” he said.

“I know.”

“They’ve got a man with a ramp.”

“You told me.”

I could hear him turning the pages of something. He always found a little job for his hands when a conversation wasn’t going well.

“Do you remember her playing it?” I asked.

“Of course I do.”

“When?”

The pages stopped. After a while he said, “When she was waiting for the potatoes.”

That was right. She played standing up, just the right hand, for as long as it took the pot to boil. Mostly songs from commercials. Once, when the plumber was in, she played the first eight bars of something grand and difficult, and I realized she knew exactly how much music she was withholding from us.

“Let the school have it,” I said.

My brother said okay, but neither of us hung up. Then he asked if I wanted the plums. I said I’d already taken four bags. He said that wasn’t an answer.

At four-forty, the woman with the pool key came back. She had listened to the recording in her car and wanted to correct something.

“It isn’t ‘cold where the sun isn’t,’” she said. “It’s ‘hold where the sun hits.’ He’s telling Gary where to stand with the cable. There was one dry patch by the rail.”

I played it through the little speakers on the counter. She leaned in. Hold where the sun hits. I could hear it now, although if I looked at my original notes, I could still hear the cold.

“Do you want me to change the transcript?”

She took a while to answer. Outside, the man who came to lock up was trying his keys in the bicycle shed. He had a bicycle of his own, a yellow one, which meant he had to lock the shed, wheel his bike to the front, lean it against the wall, lock the building, and then tuck his trouser cuff into his sock before he could go home. I’d watched him do it every weekday for eleven years.

“Put both,” she said.

So I did. I saved the file, shut the computer down, and carried my apple and the last of my things outside. At the bicycle shed, I asked the man if I could hold his bike while he locked the door. He looked surprised, then passed it to me by the saddle.

The front wheel swung round and rested against my shin. There was a bell on the handlebars, its chrome worn dull in the exact place his thumb would reach it. I’d never heard it ring. I kept my hands where they were and waited for him to finish.

**Developing a short story concept**

I'm considering writing a short story, likely around 800-1000 words, based on the theme of municipal lost property. I could create a grounded magical premise, like a city office that stores sounds. For example, a daughter discovers her mother’s silence and presents a recording. Another idea involves a man waiting in a room while helping an elderly neighbor. Maybe I'll focus on “The Undoing of a Small Bell,” involving sounds tied to memories, with a central mother-child relationship.**Crafting a layered narrative**

I want to avoid overly sentimental elements and aim for an original specificity in my story. One idea is centered on the sound of a mother dropping flour or the presence of a moth. The protagonist longs for her mother's laughter but captures ordinary pauses instead, leading to rediscovering the joy of listening to her daughter. Another promising narrative involves the last recording of a demolished swimming pool, where a municipal archivist retrieves the sound of being underwater, addressing themes of estrangement and familial connection.
